scope: Time-series observability and wallet/token relationship graph analytics
method: Pinned official repository README and license/source inspection with upstream HEAD revisions recorded. Findings are bounded research notes; no REA execution, packages installed, SYLPH code patch, build, or runtime test was performed.

provenance: Official VictoriaMetrics README and license metadata inspected at pinned default-branch commit 665c4f7e36fc017eb3451f1a7022ac3b98cc6713; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: VictoriaMetrics provides single-node and cluster time-series monitoring services, with PromQL/MetricsQL and multiple ingestion formats including Prometheus remote write and OpenTelemetry metrics.
The README describes open-source single-node and cluster variants under Apache-2.0 and separately identifies enterprise-only features.
Metrics retention, backup, and downsampling are observability features; they do not provide canonical event or trade accounting.
patterns: Export bounded-cardinality queue depth, accepted/committed rates, socket lifecycle, reconnects, and durable projection latency as metrics.
Keep measurement labels to stable dimensions such as component, provider class, and outcome; never label by mint or signature at high event volume.
overlap: Useful as a downstream metrics backend; overlaps with existing metrics/logging and must not become feed-health authority.
risks: Prometheus-style labels can create unbounded cardinality and cost.
Enterprise feature set and retention options differ from the Apache-2.0 core; confirm exact edition.
Metrics are sampled/aggregated evidence and cannot replace the durable journal.
validation: Use synthetic load only to verify exported queue, ingress, and projection-latency metrics match internal counters.
Inject missed scrapes and stale samples; verify UI continues to show canonical Engine status rather than inferred metric health.
sources.license: Apache-2.0 (single-node and cluster as described by README; enterprise features are separately identified)

provenance: Official QuestDB README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned default-branch commit ea37707be291b24a353ed2f56411fba297f4fb74; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: QuestDB is a time-series database with a write-ahead log, time-partitioned column storage, SQL, and Parquet-based data paths.
The current README describes QWP as a binary columnar WebSocket protocol for writes and Arrow query streaming; it also lists a separate line protocol path.
QuestDB is a database product rather than an in-process journal adapter, and published throughput numbers are upstream benchmarks rather than SYLPH measurements.
patterns: Benchmark telemetry or historical market-data analytics with representative event shapes and retention before choosing a separate analytical store.
Keep write path and analytics query path downstream of canonical ingress so database latency cannot delay or gate live observation handling.
overlap: Could be a separate analytics store; current canonical journal and SQLite projection handle Engine durability and should not be replaced by a second authority.
risks: A new database introduces its own WAL, backup, retention, and schema migration obligations.
QWP and other protocol compatibility must be version-pinned; benchmark claims are not evidence of SYLPH end-to-end throughput.
validation: If evaluated, compare read-after-write, restart recovery, duplicate handling, and time partition boundaries against a deterministic fixture.
Use synthetic/local data only and reconcile any execution-derived analytics to canonical fill and fee evidence.
sources.license: Apache-2.0 (repository metadata; confirm third-party and feature-specific terms before distribution)

provenance: Official SigNoz README and root LICENSE inspected at pinned default-branch commit 375b3f8305720b236a83b50955269c60d96e1f9e; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: SigNoz is an OpenTelemetry-native observability platform that correlates logs, metrics, traces, alerts, and dashboards.
The README describes community self-hosting and separately available enterprise/cloud offerings with different operational capabilities.
The root LICENSE grants MIT terms outside the `ee/` and `cmd/enterprise/` areas, which have separate license terms; the repo should not be labeled uniformly MIT without scope.
patterns: Instrument with OpenTelemetry once and correlate ingress-to-projection spans using non-sensitive request and observation IDs.
Separate alerting thresholds from the Engine’s own fail-closed readiness predicate.
overlap: Potential external view over telemetry; would duplicate pieces of the Grafana/OpenTelemetry observability resources already in the catalog.
risks: License is directory/component scoped; inspect enterprise and third-party terms before reusing or deploying those parts.
Telemetry export failure must not block journal commit or alter health/capital state.
Trace fields can expose wallet, mint, or provider data if not explicitly redacted.
validation: Use synthetic events to verify trace continuity, secret redaction, and behavior when collector/backend is unavailable.
Compare alerts to deterministic incident fixtures; prove alert state cannot flip Engine readiness.
sources.license: MIT for files outside ee/ and cmd/enterprise by root LICENSE; enterprise and third-party components have separate terms

provenance: Official Uptrace README and root LICENSE inspected at pinned default-branch commit 1e622fff165391a26bbebc135e4c4f8a843ef1bd; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: Uptrace is an OpenTelemetry APM platform for traces, metrics, and logs, with dashboards, alerting, and integrations.
The README says its storage uses ClickHouse for telemetry data and PostgreSQL for metadata, so deployment has at least two persistence components.
The root LICENSE is GNU AGPL-3.0; license review is required before network-service use or distribution.
patterns: Correlate traces, metrics, and logs with stable IDs and sampled, redacted span attributes.
Treat telemetry backends as diagnostic indexes and preserve raw canonical receipts separately.
overlap: Overlaps with SigNoz, Grafana Tempo, and other catalog observability stacks; no reason to deploy multiple without a documented selection.
risks: AGPL-3.0 obligations require legal/license review for intended deployment.
ClickHouse and PostgreSQL add separate service, backup, and access-control dependencies.
Instrumentation must not add a synchronous remote network dependency to the serial ingestion lane.
validation: If considered, send synthetic test events through an asynchronous outbox and prove remote backend failure has no effect on ingress ACKs.
Verify redaction, retention, resource consumption, and recovery of the telemetry stack.

provenance: Official HyperDX README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned default-branch commit ecddea2a0469bd53416227a79e36392dc633bff8; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: HyperDX is a ClickHouse-based observability UI that unifies logs, metrics, traces, errors, and session replay with OpenTelemetry support.
The README describes ClickStack as a composed deployment including ClickHouse, HyperDX, an OpenTelemetry Collector, and MongoDB.
The repository metadata identifies MIT licensing; the deployment is a multi-service observability stack rather than a SYLPH library.
patterns: Use cross-signal correlation and live-tail search for diagnosing synthetic queue/reconnect incidents.
Prefer OpenTelemetry-compatible instrumentation with redacted, bounded attributes and explicit sampling.
overlap: Overlaps with SigNoz, Uptrace, and Grafana components; choose one observability stack if needed rather than accumulating duplicate systems.
risks: Session replay and telemetry can capture sensitive data unless collection is explicitly restricted.
ClickStack multi-service footprint adds storage, network, credential, and upgrade dependencies.
Diagnostic UI cannot certify canonical feed health or fill settlement.
validation: Run only on synthetic/local traces first; verify privacy filters and backend outage behavior.
Keep live readiness sourced from Engine snapshot and durable incident records, not HyperDX alerts.

provenance: Official Jaeger README and license metadata inspected at pinned main commit 563e23fdb5b95e141a0ca82dad9601fa51c66ec7; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: Jaeger v2 is an OpenTelemetry Collector-based distributed tracing platform; its quick start accepts OTLP over gRPC and HTTP.
Its architecture separates SDK/collector ingestion, storage backend, query service, and UI.
The README documents backend-version support policies, so storage compatibility must be checked against the current documented support matrix.
patterns: Propagate trace context across ingress, journal commit, projection, and dashboard boundaries while keeping durable event IDs in the journal.
Use an asynchronous OTLP exporter so trace collection cannot become a synchronous dependency of the canonical ingress lane.
overlap: Overlaps with OpenTelemetry Collector, Tempo, SigNoz, Uptrace, and HyperDX; one trace backend is enough for an evaluation.
risks: Telemetry loss or stale traces do not prove a feed gap; the journal remains authoritative.
Backend support varies by version and Jaeger storage plugins introduce additional compatibility dependencies.
Sensitive identifiers in spans require redaction and sampling.
validation: Use synthetic local spans to validate trace continuity, sampling, redaction, and exporter outage behavior.
Test against the documented storage backend version support policy before deployment.

provenance: Official NetworkX README and LICENSE.txt inspected at pinned main commit 6da4704cbf32ba6f50f6d9c46cc0a071e3a87985; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: NetworkX is a Python package for creating, manipulating, and studying complex networks.
It is an offline graph-analysis library, not a graph database or Solana data source.
The pinned LICENSE.txt identifies a 3-clause BSD license.
patterns: For offline wallet research, represent observed transfers or common funding as typed, timestamped edges and preserve the source evidence for every edge.
Use graph algorithms to generate investigation candidates, then verify each relationship against canonical on-chain transactions.
overlap: Complements the graph-tooling resources in the catalog; no runtime service integration is needed.
risks: Graph edges can create false associations when based on shared infrastructure, exchange custody, or incomplete observations.
The Python implementation and memory use may be unsuitable for very large graphs or low-latency runtime.
Derived centrality/community scores are investigative signals, not risk conclusions.
validation: Use a labeled synthetic graph to test connected-component and community assumptions.
Report every edge’s source, observed time, and uncertainty; independently validate any real-world finding on chain.

provenance: Official Neo4j README and license metadata inspected at pinned 2026.09 commit 54a7dcf7c2501b31866199143364c5332da8936f; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: Neo4j describes a graph store with Cypher and ACID transactions.
The GitHub repository advertises GPL-3.0; managed Aura and separate product offerings should not be presumed to share identical terms.
A graph database could model evidence-linked wallet/token relations, but it would add a separate state store and query interface.
patterns: If used for offline research, store evidence IDs and source timestamps on each node/edge and preserve an exportable deterministic graph snapshot.
Treat graph outputs as candidate investigations; resolve economic authority in canonical chain records and Engine state.
overlap: Overlaps with Memgraph, FalkorDB, and graph libraries already in the catalog.
risks: GPL-3.0 and product/service terms require review for the exact distribution/use model.
A second state store can drift from the canonical journal and create ambiguous corrections/deletions.
Graph query results do not establish common control or malicious coordination without validated edge evidence.
validation: Before a prototype, review the intended Neo4j edition and license, then test deterministic import/export and replay from the same evidence set.
Compare graph-derived links against verified transactions and include false-positive fixtures.
sources.license: GPL-3.0 (GitHub repository metadata; verify product and deployment terms)

provenance: Official Memgraph README and root LICENSE inspected at pinned master commit 0f420c4280967268e5425c6d54f31b9155b01c0f; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: Memgraph is an in-memory, Cypher-compatible graph database implemented in C++ and positioned for real-time graph analytics.
The root LICENSE explicitly states the source is variously licensed under BSL 1.1 and the Memgraph Enterprise License, with license files under `licenses/`.
The source README and root license are insufficient to establish the exact rights for each file or an intended deployment.
patterns: If comparing graph engines, keep research ingestion asynchronous and downstream; preserve evidence IDs and edge provenance.
Run adversarial wallet-cluster fixtures to measure false positives before relying on graph relationships.
overlap: Same broad role as Neo4j/FalkorDB; do not introduce several graph databases for the same evidence set.
risks: File-level BSL/MEL terms need review before use; repository-level “open source” wording is not license approval.
In-memory operation raises persistence, backup, and restart questions for audit-linked graph data.
Graph scores may confuse common infrastructure with coordinated control.
validation: Inspect the specific files and license grants planned for use; obtain legal review if deployment rights are unclear.
Test restart/rebuild and compare graph outputs with a canonical evidence-ledger reference.
sources.license: Mixed BSL-1.1 and Memgraph Enterprise License (root LICENSE; file-specific terms must be checked)

provenance: Official FalkorDB README and root LICENSE inspected at pinned main commit b080a44c135e8b938732f155785992f39adcb41c; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: FalkorDB describes a graph database built on GraphBLAS sparse adjacency matrices and oriented toward knowledge graphs/GraphRAG.
The root LICENSE text is Server Side Public License (SSPL) version 1, not a permissive Apache license.
Its database/service deployment model makes licensing and hosting terms relevant before considering any use.
patterns: GraphBLAS is a useful reference for sparse graph computation in offline wallet-cluster analysis.
Keep source observations and derived confidence separate; a graph acceleration layer must not confer execution or risk authority.
overlap: Overlaps with NetworkX, Neo4j, Memgraph, and graph-tool; no current need for a new graph database in SYLPH runtime.
risks: SSPL-1.0 has obligations different from permissive open-source licenses; review exact intended use and service model before adopting.
A graph store can be costly to reconcile and rebuild if source evidence changes or is retracted.
Graph-derived attribution remains uncertain without verified transaction relationships.
validation: Review SSPL text and service obligations before any deployment.
Use deterministic graph fixtures and reconcile all imported edges to canonical source records; test rebuild/restart before production consideration.
sources.license: SSPL-1.0 (root LICENSE; verify obligations for intended deployment)

provenance: Official rustworkx README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned main commit 25398ab47f664962076508de27aa78ec52e24eaf; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: rustworkx is a general-purpose Python graph library implemented in Rust, exposing shortest-path and other graph operations.
The README notes that it originated to provide a faster directed graph for Qiskit but now describes broader graph-library use.
The project publishes Apache-2.0 license metadata; binary packages or source builds have platform/toolchain requirements.
patterns: For offline graph investigations, use a compact Rust-backed graph library only after profiling the data size and algorithm needs.
Preserve stable node identity and evidence-bearing edge attributes when computing connected components or paths.
overlap: Overlaps with NetworkX and igraph as a graph-algorithm library; no runtime service integration.
risks: Graph speed does not validate the input evidence or inferred relationship.
Index-based node IDs can be unstable across graph rebuilds unless a stable external identity map is maintained.
Platform binaries and Rust source builds have distinct compatibility requirements.
validation: Compare chosen algorithm output with a small hand-verified graph fixture including disconnected components and duplicate edges.
Pin package and algorithm version; verify reproducible results from the same evidence snapshot.

provenance: Official python-igraph README and GitHub license metadata inspected at pinned main commit 6188691e703fd7463e8b07076bff896fb6eae8a1; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: python-igraph is the Python interface to igraph for creating, manipulating, and analyzing large graphs.
GitHub identifies GPL-2.0 licensing; verify the exact license text and downstream package/component terms for any redistribution.
It is an offline analytical dependency, not an on-chain data provider or runtime risk evaluator.
patterns: Use graph libraries for exploratory connected-component, community, and centrality analysis on curated wallet evidence.
Keep graph-edge provenance and confidence independent from algorithm scores.
overlap: Overlaps with NetworkX and rustworkx; choose a single library based on workload and licensing, rather than including all.
risks: GPL-2.0 licensing may constrain use or distribution; confirm exact terms before incorporation.
Graph algorithms can encode misleading assumptions when edge direction, weighting, or time windows are wrong.
Large graph inputs can consume substantial memory.
validation: Create adversarial fixtures for common exchange funders, shared services, and unrelated wallets to estimate false-positive clustering.
Record code/version, algorithm parameters, graph snapshot hash, and data provenance for repeatability.
sources.license: GPL-2.0 (GitHub metadata; review pinned LICENSE and package terms before reuse)

provenance: Official Apache AGE README and Apache license metadata inspected at pinned master commit d7e2e74c95d1ac941a124437198e19b42b15446d; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: Apache AGE is a PostgreSQL extension that adds graph processing and graph queries over an existing relational database.
Its README describes graph analytics and a graph layer built on PostgreSQL, rather than a standalone low-latency market data adapter.
The repository declares Apache-2.0 licensing.
patterns: If a graph-backed research warehouse is justified, linking graph nodes to relational evidence IDs can keep provenance queryable with the underlying records.
Build graph-derived aggregates as read-only analysis and preserve the same deterministic import source.
overlap: Would add a graph extension on top of a database; overlaps with other graph engines and existing SQLite-based canonical state.
risks: Requires PostgreSQL and extension-version operations, backup, migration, and compatibility planning.
Graph transaction semantics do not establish blockchain event completeness.
A separate relational graph database would be unnecessary if existing analytics can handle the workload.
validation: Validate extension and PostgreSQL version compatibility; test deterministic import/export, restart, migration, and query results.
Reconcile all graph edges to canonical evidence and test corrections/retractions.

provenance: Official PyGraphistry README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned default-branch commit 0c71cc4bb8281ecc1f07de8657c4ec45c737a5c1; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: PyGraphistry is a Python client library for loading, shaping, embedding, and visualizing large graphs.
Its README positions visualization through the Graphistry analyzer; deployment target, data residency, and hosted versus self-hosted handling must be verified before sending wallet data.
GitHub identifies BSD-3-Clause licensing for the repository.
patterns: Use graph visualization only as an analyst-facing view over a redacted, evidence-linked graph export.
Include edge source, time, and confidence in tooltips so visual proximity is not presented as proof of common control.
overlap: Complements graph algorithms and overlaps with other graph visualization tools; not a runtime data source.
risks: Submitting graph data to a hosted analyzer can disclose wallet relationships and sensitive research; confirm deployment and data handling before use.
Visualization layout can imply stronger relationships than the underlying evidence supports.
GPU features and optional backend dependencies add environment constraints.
validation: Use synthetic or redacted graphs for any hosted/demo environment.
Test that every visible relation links to its source evidence and that uncertainty is displayed explicitly.

provenance: Official GraphFrames README and Apache license metadata inspected at pinned main commit 407773a341a344207127139c098337fa601d0275; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: GraphFrames provides DataFrame-based graph algorithms and motif queries on Apache Spark.
It is a distributed analytics package, with runtime compatibility tied to Spark, Scala, and GraphFrames versions.
The repository declares Apache-2.0 licensing.
patterns: Use distributed graph processing only when deterministic historical wallet data exceeds the practical capacity of local analysis.
Version event-time windows, edge filters, and algorithm parameters so batch graph results are reproducible.
overlap: Overlaps with NetworkX, rustworkx, igraph, and graph database options; substantially heavier and intended for larger offline workloads.
risks: Spark cluster, serialization, and version compatibility add substantial operational cost.
Distributed execution may introduce nondeterministic ordering in outputs unless results are normalized.
A graph result still needs source-level on-chain verification and cannot become trade authorization.
validation: Compare small fixtures against a single-process reference and normalize output ordering.
Test the exact Spark/Scala/GraphFrames combination and deterministic replay of the same input snapshot.
